analysis.one_liner: Expands what can be patented by wiping out court-created limits on software, genes, and natural materials.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on May 1, 2025 and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the core patent statute to narrow what courts can exclude from patenting. It keeps a short list of exclusions — pure math formulas, mental processes, genes exactly as they exist in the body, unmodified natural materials, and human-only business or artistic methods — but eliminates all judge-made exceptions built up over decades. In practice, that makes it easier to patent things like software that requires a machine to run, isolated and purified human genes, and altered natural materials, reversing Supreme Court decisions in those areas. The bill has been sitting in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since its referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Patent-holding companies and the industries built on large patent portfolios gain the most: a broader, more predictable path to patents on software implementations, isolated genes, and altered natural materials. Biotech and diagnostics firms could re-assert control over gene-based tests that courts had opened up, and tech companies and patent-licensing firms could enforce patents that are now routinely knocked out in litigation. Patent attorneys and litigators also gain from the expanded, clarified scope.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent-holding tech, biotech, and licensing firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates all judicially created exceptions to patent eligibility, replacing decades of Supreme Court and appeals-court case law with a short statutory list of excluded subject matter.

It allows patents on human genes that are purified, enriched, or otherwise altered by human activity, and on natural materials that are isolated, purified, or enriched — reversing the effect of court decisions that had denied patents on isolated genetic material.

It makes processes patentable whenever they cannot practically be performed without a machine or computer, which opens the door to patents on computer-implemented inventions that courts have invalidated under the current test.

It directs courts to weigh eligibility without discounting any claim element or asking whether elements are known, conventional, or routine, a change that makes it harder for defendants to invalidate broad patents early in a lawsuit.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and patients bear higher prices where broader patents extend monopoly pricing — most directly on gene-based diagnostic tests, where re-asserted gene patents can raise the cost of testing and block second opinions. Small software firms, startups, and app developers face more infringement lawsuits from patent-assertion companies, since a process that runs on a machine becomes patentable even if the underlying idea is a business method. Anyone sued by a patent holder loses the fast, cheap court route to invalidate a weak patent.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, patients, startups, and small developers

drawbacks.text: Allowing patents on isolated, purified human genes would reverse the current rule that natural DNA sequences cannot be owned, which consumer and medical groups have warned raises the cost of genetic testing and limits access to second opinions.

Making any process that requires a machine patentable would greatly expand software patents, including on business methods run by computers, increasing the volume of infringement suits that small developers and startups are least able to defend against.

The bill directs courts to judge eligibility without asking whether claim elements are known, conventional, or routine, which can let broad patents issue on well-known ideas that earlier doctrine would have filtered out.

A fair objection in the bill's favor is that today's eligibility test is genuinely unpredictable, producing inconsistent results that patent owners and inventors complain about, and some statutory clarification could be justified.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real problem here: the current legal test for what can be patented is widely criticized as confusing and inconsistent, and the bill retains some protections (genes as they exist in the body, purely mental processes, purely human business methods). But the specific fix swings strongly toward patent holders: it re-opens patents on isolated genes and on any computer-run process, the two areas where broader patents translate most directly into higher testing costs and more litigation against small businesses. The cost to ordinary people — in diagnostic test prices and defensive litigation — is concrete, while the benefit flows mainly to companies and law firms that already hold large patent portfolios.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced and has not moved since — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Kiley introduced the Patent Eligibility Restoration Act of 2025 on May 1, 2025, joined by Rep. Scott Peters, the bill's sole cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: the current court-built limits on patenting remain in force because the bill has not advanced. Patent holders continue to operate under existing law, and consumers have seen no change in prices or litigation exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill has not advanced

for.name: Rep. Kevin Kiley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 1, 2025; it was referred to the Judiciary Committee he serves on.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor; no opposition has been recorded because the bill has never come to a vote or a hearing.

industries.industry: Patent-holding tech companies and patent-assertion firms
industries.note: Making any process that needs a machine or computer patentable greatly expands software patents, including on business methods run by computers. The direct cost lands on small developers and startups who are the usual defendants in patent suits, and on consumers through products built around patent tolls.

The bill keeps genes exactly as they exist in the body unpatentable but allows patents on genes that are purified, enriched, or altered — effectively restoring gene patenting that courts had struck down. That can extend monopoly pricing on genetic tests and limit second opinions for patients.

A statutory eligibility test replacing decades of case law would simplify filing and enforcement work and expand the market for patent drafting and litigation. Clients' costs, not practitioners', drive the public-interest question.

Purely human business methods stay unpatentable, but any financial or business process that cannot practically run without a computer becomes eligible. Firms with large fintech patent portfolios gain enforceable claims; competitors face more infringement risk.

industries.industry: Independent software developers and small businesses
industries.note: These are the groups most often targeted by software patent suits, and the bill removes the fast court route for knocking out broad patents early in a case. Broader patentable subject matter increases their litigation exposure.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a single sponsor, one cosponsor, and no committee activity for months in a session with heavy competing business. Most one-sponsor patent bills at this stage never get a hearing and die when the Congress ends in January 2027. Passage would require the Judiciary chair to schedule a markup and leadership to bring it to the floor, neither of which is on the record.
